issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette:
Mateo Garcia has been a teacher for thirty years, but he has been a soldier for more than forty. The second career was meant to erase the first, but the body keeps its own time. At sixty-five, he finds the memories of his service are more vivid than what he ate for breakfast. It all goes back to a single afternoon in a dusty, sun-bleached country he can no longer find on a map. He was twenty-one, crammed in the back of a transport vehicle when the world dissolved into a roar of white noise and pressure. The blast threw him against the vehicle’s metal shell, and for a moment that stretched into an eternity, he was suspended in a cloud of grit and confusion. The first sensation to return was a dizzying vertigo, the world tilting on an unstable axis. The second was the taste in his mouth: a foul, coppery mix of his own blood and the pulverized earth that filled the air. He has never been able to forget that taste.

For decades, he managed. He built a new life, married, and found his calling in a special education classroom, a place of structured chaos where his patience was a balm. But the echoes of the explosion remained, shaping his world in ways he rarely admitted even to himself. His marriage frayed and then broke under the strain of his silent vigilance. His ex-wife had once told him it was like living with a ghost, a man who was physically present but whose mind was perpetually patrolling a dangerous perimeter. He never sat with his back to a door, a quirk that became an ironclad rule. Before entering any new building—a restaurant, a movie theater, even another teacher’s classroom—his mind would automatically perform a silent, swift calculation, mapping every window and exit. He had come to believe that safety was not a given state but a strategy, and he could never afford to be unprepared.

This constant state of alert has become exhausting in his classroom at Northwood Elementary. The school is a minefield of unexpected sounds. A locker slamming in the hallway can make his heart leap into his throat; a dropped textbook can cause him to flinch so violently that a student might ask if he’s okay. He is always on guard, his eyes scanning the hallway through the small window in his classroom door, his body tensed for a threat he cannot name. Last month, during a social studies lesson, a student raised his hand and asked, "Mr. Garcia, my grandpa was in the army. Were you a soldier?" Mateo opened his mouth to give a simple, practiced answer, but the act of forming the words seemed to unleash the memory. The taste of grit and copper flooded his mouth, and a dizzying wave of vertigo made the room tilt. He managed a curt nod before abruptly changing the subject, but the incident left him shaken for the rest of the day. To manage this, he has learned to position himself carefully, his desk angled near the doorway, always ensuring his path out is clear. He knows the other teachers find it odd, but the feeling of being boxed in is a specific kind of suffocation he cannot tolerate.

His triggers are insidious because they are born from inside his own body. Last Tuesday, after bending down to tie a student’s shoe, he stood up too quickly and a wave of dizziness washed over him. For a split second, the brightly coloured posters of the classroom walls blurred into a whirl of brown dust, the scent of chalk and disinfectant replaced by the smell of hot metal and sand. The feeling passed, but it left him trembling and disoriented. He has also come to dread certain foods. Anything with a strong metallic aftertaste, like canned beans, is out of the question. A few weeks ago, he bit his cheek by accident during lunch, and the sudden, warm taste of blood sent a jolt of pure panic through him, bringing back the memory with such force that he had to rush to the restroom, afraid he was going to be sick.

He has spent a lifetime avoiding strong emotions, his own and others'. He sees them as dangerous variables, unpredictable and threatening. This makes his job, working with children who often communicate through intense emotional expression, a daily challenge. When one of his students has a meltdown, a part of him wants to flee, not from the child, but from the raw feeling in the room. He resists, but the effort leaves him hollowed out. It was after a particularly difficult parent-teacher conference, where a mother’s tears of frustration made him feel a familiar, terrifying urge to bolt from the room, that he finally decided to seek help. He had to grip the sides of his chair to stay put, the conversation dissolving into a meaningless hum as he plotted his escape. He is afraid of losing control, of his body’s forty-year-old reactions finally overwhelming the life he has so carefully constructed. More than anything, Mateo just wants to feel quiet, to sit in a room and not have to know the way out.
